set1.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
set1.q: Middle ear effusion and cholesteatoma impair conduction by which mechanism?
opts: Obstruction
Obstruction blocks the canal before the drum — wax, foreign bodies, exostoses.
Mass loading
Correct. Both add fluid or tissue weight that damps movement of the tympanic membrane and ossicles. The chain is intact and mobile in principle, but it is carrying extra mass.
Stiffness effect
Stiffness is fixation rather than added weight; otosclerosis is the example.
Discontinuity
Discontinuity means the chain is physically broken, which neither of these does.

set1.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
set1.q: Which statement describes cochlear damage from long-term chronic noise exposure?
opts: Above 85 decibels, by stereocilia degeneration and apoptosis
Correct. Long-term chronic exposure to sound above 85 decibels induces irreversible stereocilia degeneration and apoptosis of the acoustic hair cells.
Above 85 decibels, causing reversible stereocilia fatigue
The threshold is right but the change is not reversible — apoptosis is cell death.
Above 120 decibels, causing tympanic membrane rupture
Tympanic membrane rupture is not the chronic lesion. Long-term exposure above 85 decibels causes irreversible stereocilia degeneration and hair cell apoptosis.
Above 60 decibels, causing endolymphatic hydrops
Endolymphatic hydrops is the lesion of Meniere disease, caused by defective resorption rather than by sound exposure at any level.

set1.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
set1.q: Which description fits conductive hearing loss?
opts: Destruction of hair cells or auditory nerve fibers, in the inner ear
That is sensorineural loss, sited in the cochlea or cranial nerve VIII. Conductive loss is defective sound wave transmission to the oval window from the external or middle ear.
Failure of glutamate release at cranial nerve VIII
Glutamate release onto cranial nerve VIII is a step beyond the conducting apparatus, so its failure is sensorineural. The conductive defect lies in the external or middle ear.
Defective sound transmission, in the external or middle ear
Correct. The apparatus that carries sound inward has failed; the cochlea and nerve are intact. That anatomical split is what the tuning fork tests are detecting.
Central processing failure in the auditory cortex
Central auditory pathways are grouped with sensorineural loss, alongside the cochlea and cranial nerve VIII. Conductive loss sits in the external or middle ear.

set1.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
set1.q: Why does asymmetrical vestibular input produce a false sense of motion?
opts: The cochlea sends conflicting auditory signals
The cochlea handles hearing and contributes nothing to the sense of position or movement.
The brain reads the mismatch between the two sides as movement
Correct. Balance is a comparison, so unequal input is indistinguishable from turning.
Cerebral perfusion falls on one side
Falling cerebral perfusion produces dizziness and presyncope, which is the category vertigo is separated from.
The otoliths dissolve
Otoconia do not dissolve. They can become dislodged into the semicircular canals, which is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.

set1.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
set1.q: What is the pattern of onset in presbycusis?
opts: Gradual, symmetrical and bilateral
Correct, and it is sensorineural. Asymmetry would point away from aging toward a focal lesion.
Sudden and unilateral
Sudden unilateral sensorineural loss fits labyrinthitis. Presbycusis is gradual, symmetrical and bilateral in older adults.
Episodic and fluctuating
Loss that comes and goes suggests Meniere disease, where endolymph pressure rises and falls.
Gradual but strictly unilateral
Presbycusis is symmetrical and bilateral, not one-sided; its gradual loss begins with the high-frequency tones.

set1.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
set1.q: How do the causes of anterior and posterior epistaxis differ?
opts: Anterior from local trauma and dry air; posterior from hypertension and anticoagulation
Correct. Anterior bleeds are local and mechanical; posterior bleeds reflect a systemic vascular or clotting problem, which is also why they are more profuse and carry airway risk.
Anterior from hypertension and anticoagulation; posterior from digital trauma
The two etiologies are swapped. Digital trauma and dry air are anterior causes; hypertension and anticoagulation drive posterior bleeds.
Both are caused predominantly by anticoagulation
Anticoagulation belongs with the posterior group; anterior bleeds are usually local.
Anterior from coagulopathy; posterior from low humidity
Reversed again: coagulopathy belongs with posterior bleeding and low humidity with anterior mucosal drying.

set1.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
set1.q: Which demographic and inheritance profile fits otosclerosis?
opts: Commonest in older males, with no hereditary component
Both halves are wrong: the peak is younger and female, and half of cases are autosomal dominant.
Commonest in children, autosomal recessive
Neither half matches: otosclerosis peaks in young to middle-aged women, and half of cases are autosomal dominant rather than recessive.
Young-to-middle-aged females, accelerated by pregnancy; 50% autosomal dominant
Correct. Otosclerosis is most common in young-to-middle-aged females and is accelerated by pregnancy; 50 percent of cases are autosomal dominant with variable penetrance.
Commonest in young females but entirely sporadic
The demographic is right, but it is not sporadic: 50 percent of cases are autosomal dominant, with variable penetrance.

set1.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set1.q: Why are nasal polyps classed as non-neoplastic?
opts: They are malignant but slow growing
Polyps are benign and not neoplastic at all, so describing them as slow-growing malignancy is wrong twice over.
No new tissue is grown; existing mucosa becomes edematous
Correct. Nasal polyps are benign edematous masses of the mucous membranes of the sinus ostia or ethmoid air cells, not new neoplastic tissue.
They arise from cartilage rather than epithelium
They arise from the mucous membranes of the sinus ostia or ethmoid air cells.
They regress without treatment in every case
Regression is not what the term means. Polyps are non-neoplastic because no new tissue grows: they are benign edematous masses of existing mucous membrane.

set1.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
set1.q: Which nodal findings require immediate assessment to exclude lymphoma?
opts: Tender mobile nodes during a viral upper respiratory infection
Tender nodes during a viral upper respiratory infection are reactive enlargement responding to regional infection, usually benign.
Bilateral small nodes in a child with otitis media
Nodes responding to otitis media are reactive enlargement from a regional head and neck infection, usually benign.
Persistent rubbery or matted nodes in older adults
Correct. Reactive nodes are usually tender and follow a regional infection. Rubbery, matted, persistent and supraclavicular in an older patient is the combination that changes the level of concern.
Any palpable cervical node at all
Palpable nodes are common and usually reactive. Persistent rubbery or matted nodes in older adults are what require assessment for lymphoma.

set1.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
set1.q: Which definitions of acute and chronic rhinosinusitis are accurate?
opts: Acute under 2 weeks; chronic beyond 6 weeks, often with septal deviation
Neither threshold matches: acute rhinosinusitis lasts under 4 weeks, and chronic lasts over 12 weeks despite therapy, often with nasal polyps.
Acute under 4 weeks; chronic beyond 12 weeks despite therapy, often with nasal polyps
Correct. The two thresholds are the definition. Acute disease is usually viral — rhinovirus or influenza — with secondary bacterial infection by Streptococcus pneumoniae or Haemophilus influenzae.
Acute under 12 weeks; chronic beyond 6 months, often with turbinate hypertrophy
The thresholds are wrong: acute rhinosinusitis is under 4 weeks and chronic is beyond 12 weeks despite therapy.
Acute under 4 weeks; chronic beyond 12 weeks, usually with no mucosal change
The durations are right but chronic disease often comes WITH polyps rather than without change.

set1.io: Objective 1 — Review the anatomy of the ear, nose, neck and throat system.
set1.q: Which description fits the semicircular canals?
opts: Linear acceleration and gravitational position, via the otoliths
That is the utricle and saccule — the otolith organs — which handle static and linear balance.
Rotational acceleration, by endolymph bending the cupula
Correct. Three loops in the sagittal, coronal and transverse planes. The fluid lags behind the head, the gelatinous cupula bends, and the hair cell stereocilia inside it are stimulated.
Sound frequency, via the basilar membrane
Sound is transduced by the cochlea, which converts fluid displacement into neural signals through the organ of Corti.
Middle ear pressure, via the Eustachian tube
The Eustachian tube equalizes middle ear pressure. That is a conduction function and has nothing to do with detecting head movement.

set1.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
set1.q: Why does presbycusis make voices hard to discriminate in noisy environments?
opts: Low frequencies go first, taking the vowels
Low-tone loss is the pattern of Meniere disease. Presbycusis starts at the high frequencies, taking consonants such as /s/, /f/ and /t/.
All frequencies fall equally
Presbycusis is not a flat loss. It begins with the high-frequency tones that carry speech consonants such as /s/, /f/ and /t/.
Only frequencies above the speech range are affected
The lost high-frequency tones lie within speech: consonants such as /s/, /f/ and /t/, which is why voice discrimination suffers.
High frequencies go first, taking the speech consonants
Correct. Presbycusis begins with high-frequency tones, which include speech consonants such as /s/, /f/ and /t/, making voice discrimination difficult in noisy environments.

set1.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set1.q: Which single event in otosclerosis produces the hearing loss?
opts: Ankylosis of the stapes footplate
Correct. Once the footplate is fixed it cannot transfer mechanical vibration into the cochlear fluid, and conduction fails progressively. Fixation is the whole lesion.
Erosion of the incus by the remodeled bone
Erosion of the incus would be discontinuity. Otosclerosis works by fixation: ankylosis of the stapes footplate in the oval window halts vibration transfer.
Hair cell loss at the cochlear base
Hair cell loss from the cochlear base is aminoglycoside damage and gives sensorineural loss. Otosclerosis is a conductive lesion of the stapes footplate.
Accumulation of endolymph in the scala media
Fluid accumulating in the scala media is endolymphatic hydrops in Meniere disease, a sensorineural and vestibular problem rather than a conductive one.

set1.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
set1.q: What drives dizziness or lightheadedness, as distinct from vertigo?
opts: Asymmetrical input between the two vestibular apparatus
Asymmetrical vestibular input is the mechanism of vertigo itself, which is the thing dizziness has to be distinguished FROM.
Dislodged otoconia in the semicircular canals
Dislodged otoconia cause benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, a vestibular cause of true vertigo rather than of lightheadedness.
Endolymphatic hydrops
Endolymphatic hydrops is Meniere disease, which is vestibular — so it produces vertigo rather than the presyncopal sensation of dizziness.
Cerebral hypoperfusion or metabolic imbalance
Correct. Dizziness is a non-vestibular sensation of impending faint or unsteadiness, driven by cerebral hypoperfusion, orthostatic hypotension or metabolic imbalance.

set1.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
set1.q: Which description defines vertigo as distinct from dizziness?
opts: A sensation of impending faint from cerebral hypoperfusion
That is dizziness or presyncope, driven by hypoperfusion, orthostatic hypotension or metabolic imbalance.
Any unsteadiness on standing
Unsteadiness alone does not distinguish the two; the hallucination of motion does.
Loss of consciousness preceded by spinning
Vertigo explicitly involves NO syncope. Loss of consciousness points away from a vestibular cause and toward cerebral hypoperfusion.
A hallucination of motion, with NO syncope
Correct. Asymmetry between the two sides is the mechanism, and the absence of syncope is the separator. Dizziness or lightheadedness is a non-vestibular sensation of impending faint.

set1.io: Objective 1 — Review the anatomy of the ear, nose, neck and throat system.
set1.q: What makes the middle ear vulnerable to the pressure changes behind otitis media?
opts: It is fluid-filled and cannot compress
The middle ear is air-filled; the INNER ear holds the fluid.
It is an air-filled space vented only by the Eustachian tube
Correct. A sealed air pocket with one vent is why closing the vent drops the pressure and draws in fluid.
It has no blood supply
Blood supply is not the weakness. The middle ear is air-filled, and when the Eustachian tube fails to open, its mucosa absorbs oxygen and nitrogen, creating negative pressure.
It is lined by keratinized skin
A keratinized lining is not the problem. It is the middle ear mucosa that absorbs oxygen and nitrogen when the Eustachian tube fails to open, so pressure falls.

set1.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set1.q: Which molecular pathway drives nasal polyp formation?
opts: Interleukins 1, 6 and tumor necrosis factor, with neutrophil influx
Neutrophil-driven cytokines do not form polyps. Polyps come from type 2 inflammation: interleukins 4, 5 and 13 with tissue eosinophil influx.
Interferon gamma, with lymphocyte influx
Interferon gamma with lymphocytes is not the polyp pathway, which is type 2 inflammation with interleukins 4, 5 and 13 and eosinophils.
Interleukins 4, 5 and 13, with eosinophil influx
Correct. Chronic type 2 allergic responses release interleukins 4, 5 and 13 and draw eosinophils into the tissue, forming benign edematous masses from the sinus ostia or ethmoid air cells.
Interleukin 17, with mast cell influx
Interleukin 17 and mast cell influx are not the polyp pathway. Polyps are type 2 inflammation driven by interleukins 4, 5 and 13 with eosinophils.

set1.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set1.q: What happens to the wider nasal cavity opposite a septal deviation?
opts: Compensatory inferior turbinate hypertrophy
Correct. The contralateral wide cavity undergoes compensatory inferior turbinate enlargement to humidify the increased volume of air passing through it.
It atrophies from disuse
The opposite happens. The wide side carries MORE airflow, so its turbinate enlarges to condition the extra volume rather than wasting away.
It develops polyps from the increased flow
Polyps arise from type 2 inflammation, not from airflow volume.
Nothing changes; only the narrow side is affected
The wide side does change: its inferior turbinate undergoes compensatory hypertrophy to humidify the increased air volume.

set1.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
set1.q: Which statement about bacterial tonsillitis and its abscess complication is accurate?
opts: Streptococcus pneumoniae; bilateral exudate
Streptococcus pneumoniae causes otitis media and rhinosinusitis, and tonsillar exudate is a symptom of ordinary tonsillitis, not of abscess.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa; fever above 39 degrees
Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes otitis externa, and fever is a symptom of uncomplicated tonsillitis rather than a sign of abscess.
Haemophilus influenzae; odynophagia
Haemophilus is on the otitis media and sinusitis lists, and odynophagia is present in uncomplicated tonsillitis too.
Group A Streptococcus; asymmetric deviation with trismus
Correct. Tonsillitis is usually Group A Streptococcus, and asymmetric tonsillar deviation with trismus indicates a complicating tonsillar abscess.

set1.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set1.q: Which ion movement depolarizes the cochlear hair cell?
opts: Efflux into the perilymph through voltage-gated channels
Voltage-gated channels open only AFTER depolarization, triggering glutamate release. The depolarizing event is influx from the endolymph through the tip-link channels.
Influx from the endolymph through the tip-link channels

Correct. Deflected stereocilia open the tip-link channels, permitting rapid influx from the endolymph into the hair cell. Depolarization then opens voltage-gated channels and glutamate is released onto cranial nerve VIII.
Influx from the perilymph across the basilar membrane
The depolarizing influx comes from the endolymph, through tip-link channels opened by stereocilia deflection, not from the perilymph across the basilar membrane.
Release from intracellular stores after glutamate binding
Glutamate is what the hair cell RELEASES onto cranial nerve VIII after it depolarizes. It is the output of the cell, not a signal arriving at it.

set1.io: Objective 1 — Review the anatomy of the ear, nose, neck and throat system.
set1.q: Which structure separates the external ear from the middle ear?
opts: The oval window, which passes energy to the cochlea
The oval window is the boundary between MIDDLE and INNER ear, driven by the stapes.
The round window, which relieves pressure
The round window is not the external boundary. The tympanic membrane separates external from middle ear, vibrating to pass sound energy to the ossicles.
The Eustachian tube, which equalizes pressure
The Eustachian tube equalizes middle ear pressure; it vents the middle ear rather than separating it from the external ear.
The tympanic membrane, which vibrates and passes energy to the ossicles
Correct. It is the boundary and the first moving part of the conducting chain, which is why perforating it causes conductive loss.

set1.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set1.q: Why does the vertigo of Meniere disease come in attacks rather than continuously?
opts: Pressure builds until micro-ruptures occur, then re-equilibrates
Correct. Defective resorption lets endolymph accumulate and balloon the scala media until micro-ruptures occur; that build-up and release makes it episodic.
The virus replicates in waves
Meniere disease is a disorder of endolymph resorption, not an infection, so there is no organism replicating.
Otoconia settle between episodes
Otoconia settling between episodes explains benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which lasts seconds rather than hours.
Inflammation resolves and recurs
Inflammation across the canals and cochlea is labyrinthitis, whose vertigo lasts days and improves over weeks.

set1.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set1.q: How do cisplatin and carboplatin cause permanent bilateral sensorineural loss?
opts: They generate reactive oxygen species that destroy outer hair cells at the cochlear base
Reactive oxygen species destroying outer hair cells from the cochlear base is the aminoglycoside mechanism, and it takes the high frequencies first.
They inhibit prestin in outer hair cells
That is salicylate, and the effect is tinnitus rather than permanent loss.
They cross-link DNA in stria vascularis cells, compromising endolymph ion homeostasis
Correct. The stria vascularis maintains the ionic composition of endolymph, and without that gradient transduction fails. Damage there is permanent and bilateral.
They fix the stapes footplate in the oval window
That is otosclerosis, a conductive lesion with no drug involvement.

set1.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
set1.q: Which statement about the causes of otitis externa is accurate?
opts: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae; fungal disease follows swimming
Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae are otitis media organisms. Fungal otitis externa follows prolonged antibiotic use or hyperhumid conditions.
Moraxella catarrhalis alone; fungal disease follows trauma
Moraxella catarrhalis sits on the otitis MEDIA list alongside Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, not in the external canal.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus; fungal after antibiotics
Correct. Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus cause 80 to 90 percent of cases; fungal disease from Aspergillus niger or Candida albicans often follows prolonged antibiotic use.
Respiratory syncytial virus and rhinovirus; fungal disease follows steroid use
Respiratory syncytial virus and rhinovirus are viral causes of otitis MEDIA; they are not what colonizes an external canal.

set1.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
set1.q: Which set of causes belongs to sensorineural rather than conductive loss?
opts: Presbycusis, ototoxic drugs, noise trauma and acoustic neuroma
Correct. All four damage the cochlea or the nerve. Note acoustic neuroma sits here because cranial nerve VIII is part of the sensorineural pathway even though the tumor is outside the cochlea.
Cerumen impaction, otosclerosis, otitis media and tympanic membrane perforation
All four are conductive — they obstruct, load, stiffen or interrupt the sound-conducting apparatus.
Cholesteatoma, exostoses, foreign body and ossicular necrosis
All four are conductive: foreign bodies and exostoses obstruct the canal, cholesteatoma adds mass loading, and ossicular necrosis breaks the ossicular chain.
Eustachian tube dysfunction, middle ear effusion and stapes fixation
All three are conductive: effusion loads the drum with mass, and stapes fixation stiffens the chain. None involves the cochlea or the nerve.

set1.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set1.q: Which two ototoxic effects are reversible or symptom-limited rather than permanent?
opts: Gentamicin and tobramycin damage
Gentamicin and tobramycin generate reactive oxygen species that destroy outer hair cells from the cochlear base, a destructive rather than reversible effect.
Cisplatin and carboplatin damage
Cisplatin and carboplatin cross-link DNA in stria vascularis cells and cause bilateral permanent sensorineural loss.
Noise trauma and presbycusis
Both are irreversible — noise causes stereocilia degeneration and hair cell apoptosis.
Furosemide on the strial potential; salicylate on prestin
Correct. The loop diuretic effect on the strial potential is reversible, and the salicylate effect on the outer hair cell motor protein produces tinnitus. Neither destroys the cells outright.

set1.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set1.q: Why does prolonged antibiotic use predispose to FUNGAL otitis externa?
opts: It thins the canal skin directly
Antibiotics do not thin the canal skin. What they remove is the bacterial competition.
It removes the bacterial competition that normally limits fungal growth
Correct. Prolonged antibiotic use suppresses the bacteria, and Aspergillus niger or Candida albicans then take over as fungal otitis externa.
It raises the canal pH to favor fungi
The association is not explained by pH. It is the loss of competing bacteria that lets fungus grow.
It damages the tympanic membrane
Otitis externa is an infection of the canal. Its fungal form follows prolonged antibiotic use or hyperhumid conditions, not membrane damage.

set1.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
set1.q: Which way does the nystagmus of labyrinthitis beat?
opts: Horizontal-rotary, with the fast phase beating TOWARD the affected side
The direction is reversed; the fast phase beats away from the lesion.
Vertical and non-suppressible
Vertical nystagmus is a central feature, and labyrinthitis is peripheral.
Absent, because hearing rather than balance is affected
Labyrinthitis impairs both hearing and balance, and it presents with horizontal-rotary nystagmus and gait ataxia.
Horizontal-rotary, with the fast phase beating AWAY from the affected side
Correct. Labyrinthitis gives horizontal-rotary nystagmus with the fast phase beating away from the affected side, with severe postural instability, gait ataxia and nausea.

set1.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set1.q: What is the mechanism of Meniere disease?
opts: Defective endolymph resorption causing hydrops, ballooning the scala media until micro-ruptures occur
Correct. Endolymphatic hydrops is the lesion: fluid accumulates because it is not resorbed, the membranous labyrinth distends, and micro-ruptures follow. The episodic nature follows from that cycle.
Inflammatory swelling and vascular congestion of the labyrinth after a viral infection
That is labyrinthitis, and the recent upper respiratory infection is what separates the two clinically.
Dislodged otoconia floating in the semicircular canals
Otoconia loose in the semicircular canals is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which produces brief positional attacks and spares hearing.
Demyelination of the vestibular nerve
Meniere disease is not demyelinating. Its lesion is endolymphatic hydrops, from defective endolymph resorption distending the membranous labyrinth.

set1.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set1.q: Why does anticoagulation favor POSTERIOR rather than anterior epistaxis?
opts: The anterior septum has no blood supply
Kiesselbach's plexus supplies the anterior septum richly, which is exactly why anterior bleeds are the common ones.
Anticoagulants are concentrated posteriorly
No regional concentration is involved. Anticoagulant therapy sits with hypertension, atherosclerosis and coagulopathy as the systemic causes of posterior bleeds.
Posterior bleeding is driven by systemic vascular and clotting factors
Correct. Anterior causes are local insults to the mucosa; posterior causes act on the vessels and on clotting.
The posterior mucosa is thinner
Mucosal thickness is not what separates the two. The difference is local insult against systemic vascular and clotting factors.

set2.io: Objective 1 — Review the anatomy of the ear, nose, neck and throat system.
set2.q: Which statement describes the source of anterior epistaxis?
opts: Woodruff's plexus on the posterolateral wall, about 90 percent
Woodruff's plexus on the posterolateral wall is the posterior source, about 10 percent of cases, not the anterior 90 percent.
Kiesselbach's plexus on the anterior septum, about 90 percent
Correct. Anterior epistaxis, 90 percent of cases, comes from Kiesselbach's plexus on the anterior septum; the posterior 10 percent come from Woodruff's plexus on the posterolateral wall.
The sphenopalatine artery, about 50 percent
The sphenopalatine artery is not the anterior source. Anterior bleeds, 90 percent of cases, come from Kiesselbach's plexus on the anterior septum.
The anterior ethmoidal artery, about 10 percent
Posterior bleeds are the 10 percent, and they come from Woodruff's plexus; anterior bleeds come from Kiesselbach's plexus on the anterior septum.

set2.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
set2.q: Why does cerumen impaction cause conductive rather than sensorineural loss?
opts: It blocks the canal, so sound never reaches the conducting chain
Correct. The cochlea is untouched, and the defect is purely one of delivery.
It damages the outer hair cells
Wax sits in the canal and never reaches the cochlea, so the hair cells are untouched by it.
It stiffens the stapes footplate
Stiffening of the stapes footplate is otosclerosis, a separate conductive mechanism entirely.
It loads the tympanic membrane with fluid
Wax sits in the canal in front of the drum. Fluid loading the tympanic membrane is middle ear effusion, a mass-loading mechanism.

set2.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
set2.q: Which pair of tuning fork findings indicates conductive hearing loss?
opts: Weber to the AFFECTED ear; Rinne shows bone conduction greater than air
Correct. With sound wave transmission to the oval window defective, Weber lateralizes to the AFFECTED ear and Rinne is abnormal, with bone conduction greater than air.
Weber to the UNAFFECTED ear; Rinne shows air conduction greater than bone
That is the sensorineural pattern: the damaged cochlea cannot hear either route well, so Weber goes to the better ear and Rinne keeps its normal ratio.
Weber to the affected ear; Rinne shows air conduction greater than bone
The Weber is right but Rinne is not — a normal air-over-bone ratio means the conducting apparatus is working.
Weber is equal; Rinne shows bone greater than air bilaterally
An equal Weber implies no lateralizing lesion. In conductive loss Weber lateralizes to the affected ear, and Rinne there shows bone greater than air.

set2.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
set2.q: Which history most separates labyrinthitis from Meniere disease?
opts: Unilateral rather than bilateral symptoms
Laterality does not separate them: labyrinthitis gives unilateral tinnitus and hearing loss, and Meniere disease gives fullness in the affected ear.
The presence of tinnitus
Both labyrinthitis and Meniere disease produce tinnitus, so its presence tells you nothing about which one you are looking at.
A recent upper respiratory infection
Correct. Labyrinthitis is caused by viral infection, typically a recent viral upper respiratory infection, whereas Meniere disease arises from defective endolymph resorption causing hydrops.
The presence of sensorineural hearing loss
Both cause it. The duration of vertigo and the preceding infection are what differ.

set2.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set2.q: Where do the pressure waves that begin hearing actually travel first?
opts: The scala tympani
The scala tympani carries the wave later in its course, after it has passed the cochlear duct.
The cochlear duct itself
The duct holds the endolymph that is displaced, but the wave begins in the scala vestibuli.
The scala vestibuli
Correct. Stapes movement at the oval window starts them there, and they displace endolymph in the cochlear duct.
The semicircular canals
The semicircular canals detect rotation and play no part in transmitting sound to the organ of Corti.

set2.io: Objective 1 — Review the anatomy of the ear, nose, neck and throat system.
set2.q: What protects the outer third of the ear canal?
opts: Mucus from goblet cells
Mucus is not the canal's protection. Ceruminous glands produce protective cerumen, and the outer third of the canal also carries protective hair follicles.
Ciliated epithelium sweeping debris outward
The ear canal is not protected by cilia. Its outer third is protected by cerumen from ceruminous glands and by hair follicles.
A keratin plug at the isthmus
There is no keratin plug at the isthmus. What sits in the outer third is cerumen and hair.
Cerumen from ceruminous glands, and hair follicles
Correct. Ceruminous glands produce protective cerumen, and the outer third of the canal also has protective hair follicles.

set2.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set2.q: Which description fits vocal cord polyps, as distinct from nodules?
opts: Bilateral fibrous calluses from chronic phonotrauma
Bilateral fibrous calluses from chronic phonotrauma are NODULES. Polyps differ on every count — unilateral, soft, and from one event.
Bilateral soft lesions at the anterior commissure from reflux
Neither matches: polyps are unilateral on the middle third and follow acute strain, not bilateral at the commissure from reflux.
Unilateral, soft and pedunculated on the middle third, after one severe strain
Correct. One event rather than chronic repetition, and the healing response is inflammatory rather than a callus. Site and laterality both differ from nodules.
Unilateral fibrous calluses from chronic yelling
This mixes the two lesions. Calluses from chronic trauma are nodules and they are bilateral; polyps are unilateral and follow a single event.

set2.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set2.q: Which description fits allergic rhinitis?
opts: IgG-mediated type 2 hypersensitivity with purulent rhinorrhea
Purulent discharge points to bacterial rhinosinusitis. Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated type 1 reaction with clear rhinorrhea and nasal itching.
Immune complex deposition, type 3 hypersensitivity
Immune complex deposition is type 3 hypersensitivity. Allergic rhinitis is type 1, immediate and IgE-mediated on the nasal mucosa.
T cell mediated, type 4 delayed hypersensitivity
Allergic rhinitis is not a delayed T cell reaction. It is an IgE-mediated type 1 hypersensitivity of the nasal mucosa triggered by inhaled allergens.
IgE-mediated type 1 hypersensitivity, with CLEAR rhinorrhea

Correct. Type 1 hypersensitivity driven by IgE (immunoglobulin E) against inhaled allergens. The CLEAR discharge separates it from bacterial sinusitis, which is purulent. Allergic shiners complete the picture.

set2.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set2.q: Which physical law explains why a small septal deviation causes disproportionate obstruction?
opts: Fick's law of diffusion
Fick's law is not the one that applies. Poiseuille's law is: even a small narrowing of the airway dramatically increases resistance to airflow.
Laplace's law
Laplace's law does not account for the obstruction. By Poiseuille's law, small airway narrowing sharply raises resistance, producing unilateral resistance.
Boyle's law
Boyle's law does not explain nasal obstruction. Poiseuille's law does: even small airway narrowing dramatically increases resistance to airflow.
Poiseuille's law
Correct. By Poiseuille's law even small airway narrowing dramatically increases resistance, so a modest deviation can produce unilateral resistance and chronic nasal obstruction.

set2.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
set2.q: A temporal bone fracture causes conductive loss by which mechanism?
opts: Discontinuity of the ossicular chain
Correct. The chain is physically disrupted so the wave cannot be conducted across it. Ossicular necrosis produces the same end result by erosion rather than trauma.
Stiffness of the ossicular chain
Stiffness is impaired mobility of the ossicles or drum, as in otosclerosis. A temporal bone fracture instead physically disrupts the ossicular chain.
Mass loading of the tympanic membrane
Mass loading requires added fluid or tissue weight damping the chain. A fracture removes continuity rather than adding weight.
Obstruction of the external canal
Obstruction blocks the external canal before the drum. A temporal bone fracture acts deeper, on the ossicular chain itself.

set2.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
set2.q: Which causes produce CENTRAL vertigo?
opts: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, Meniere disease and labyrinthitis
Those are peripheral causes involving the inner ear, along with vestibular neuritis. Central causes involve the brainstem or cerebellum.
Brainstem stroke, multiple sclerosis and cerebellar tumor
Correct. All involve the brainstem or cerebellum, which is why the nystagmus can be vertical and is not suppressed by fixation, and why other neurological signs appear.
Otosclerosis and cerumen impaction
Otosclerosis and cerumen impaction are conductive hearing problems. Neither involves the vestibular apparatus, so neither causes vertigo at all.
Presbycusis and noise trauma
Both are sensorineural hearing loss without a vestibular component.

set2.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set2.q: Why does labyrinthitis impair hearing AND balance together?
opts: Defective endolymph resorption ballooning the scala media
That is the hydrops of Meniere disease, and it does not begin with inflammation.
Dislodged otoconia striking structures in the endolymph
That is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which spares hearing entirely.
Fixation of the stapes footplate
Fixation of the stapes footplate is otosclerosis, a conductive middle ear lesion with no vestibular component.
Inflammation across both the semicircular canals and the cochlea
Correct. Inflammatory swelling, vascular congestion and endolymphatic disruption affect the semicircular canals and the cochlea at once, impairing balance and the organ of Corti together.

set2.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
set2.q: Why are there three semicircular canals rather than one?
opts: Each detects a different speed of rotation
The three canals are distinguished by the plane they occupy, not by the speed of rotation they detect.
Two detect rotation and one detects gravity
Gravity and linear acceleration are the otolith organs' job.
Redundancy in case one is damaged
Redundancy is not the explanation. Three canals exist because rotation happens in three planes.
They sit in three planes, so rotation in any direction is detected
Correct. Sagittal, coronal and transverse between them cover all rotational movement.

set2.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
set2.q: What does it mean, structurally, for lymph nodes to be MATTED?
opts: They have lost their individual capsules and move as one mass
Correct. Matted nodes move together as one mass, and persistent rubbery or matted nodes in older adults require assessment to rule out lymphoma.
They are tender and mobile
Tender and mobile describes a reactive node responding to local infection, which is the reassuring picture.
They are smaller than normal
Matting is about nodes moving together as one mass, and says nothing about whether they are large or small.
They fluctuate in size with infection
Nodes that swell and settle with infection are behaving reactively, which is the opposite of the concerning pattern.

set2.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
set2.q: Which organisms most commonly cause bacterial otitis media?
opts: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis
Correct. The classic middle ear trio. Viral causes are respiratory syncytial virus, rhinovirus, influenza and adenovirus.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus
Those are the otitis EXTERNA organisms, accounting for 80 to 90 percent of that condition.
Aspergillus niger and Candida albicans
Those are the fungal otitis externa organisms, often after prolonged antibiotics or humid conditions.
Group A Streptococcus alone
That is the usual bacterial cause of tonsillitis, not of otitis media.

set2.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set2.q: Which description fits inferior turbinate hypertrophy?
opts: Cartilage displacement off the midline; a congenital deformity
Cartilage displaced off the midline is a deviated septum, which divides the nasal cavity into asymmetric flow channels.
Venous engorgement, edema or bony hypertrophy; decongestant rebound
Correct. The inferior turbinates enlarge from venous sinusoid engorgement, mucosal edema or bony hypertrophy; rebound hyperemia from topical decongestants is rhinitis medicamentosa.
Eosinophilic polyp formation; an allergic reaction
Eosinophilic masses are nasal polyps from type 2 inflammation. Turbinate enlargement comes from engorgement, edema or bony hypertrophy.
Bacterial infection of the turbinate bone; osteomyelitis
Turbinates do not enlarge from bone infection. The triggers are allergic rhinitis, vasomotor instability and rebound hyperemia from topical decongestants.

set2.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set2.q: What is the bone remodeling sequence in otosclerosis?
opts: Osteoblastic overgrowth of dense cortical bone without resorption
The sequence begins with osteoclastic resorption, and the bone laid down is hypervascular spongy osteoid, not dense cortical overgrowth.
Osteoclastic resorption, then spongy osteoid replacement
Correct. Abnormal osteoclastic bone resorption is followed by hypervascular spongy osteoid replacement around the otic capsule and stapes footplate, which then fixes the footplate.
Demineralization of the ossicles from chronic inflammation
Otosclerosis is not an inflammatory demineralization. It is osteoclastic resorption followed by spongy osteoid replacement around the stapes footplate.
Fibrous scarring of the round window membrane
The lesion is at the oval window and the stapes footplate, and it is bone rather than scar.

set2.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set2.q: What is the sequence by which Eustachian tube dysfunction creates negative middle ear pressure?
opts: The tube fails to open, so the mucosa absorbs the gases
Correct. The middle ear is an air-filled space; if it is not re-ventilated, the mucosa absorbs the gases and the pressure falls. That negative pressure is the start of the otitis media sequence.
Mucus production increases faster than the tube can drain it
The initiating step is not mucus overproduction. The tube fails to open, so oxygen and nitrogen are absorbed into the mucosa and middle ear pressure falls.
Bacterial infection erodes the tube lining and opens it permanently
The problem is not a tube held open. Negative pressure arises because the tube fails to open periodically, letting the mucosa absorb oxygen and nitrogen.
The tympanic membrane becomes stiff and pulls the ossicles inward
The drum is not the starting point. Failure of the tube to open lets the mucosa absorb oxygen and nitrogen, creating negative middle ear pressure.

set2.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set2.q: What is canalithiasis?
opts: Calcification of the stapes footplate
Calcification fixing the stapes footplate is otosclerosis, a conductive lesion of the middle ear with no vestibular component.
Dislodged otoconia floating free in the semicircular canals

Correct. Canalithiasis means dislodged otoconia, the crystals, lying in the semicircular canals; the result is episodic vertigo, usually under a minute, with head position changes and no hearing loss.
Accumulation of endolymph in the membranous labyrinth
Endolymph accumulating in the membranous labyrinth is the hydrops of Meniere disease, which gives hours-long attacks with hearing loss.
Inflammatory debris within the cochlea after infection
Inflammation within the cochlea is labyrinthitis, which impairs hearing. Canalithiasis causes NO hearing loss.

set2.io: Objective 1 — Review the anatomy of the ear, nose, neck and throat system.
set2.q: Which structures detect linear acceleration and gravitational position?
opts: The three semicircular canals
The semicircular canals detect ROTATIONAL acceleration through cupula deflection. Linear and gravitational sensing belongs to the otoliths.
The otolith organs
Correct. They handle static and linear balance, while the semicircular canals handle rotation. The two systems together give the brain a complete picture of head position and movement.
The cupula and ampulla
Those are the sensing apparatus inside the semicircular canals, so again rotational.
The organ of Corti
The organ of Corti transduces sound into neural signals. It is the hearing apparatus and plays no part in equilibrium.

set2.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
set2.q: What is the classic symptom tetrad of Meniere disease?
opts: Continuous vertigo lasting days, unilateral tinnitus, unilateral loss, and nystagmus
That is labyrinthitis, whose vertigo lasts days and improves over weeks, against the hours-long episodes of Meniere disease.
Vertigo lasting under a minute on head movement, with no hearing loss
Otoconia loose in the semicircular canals is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which produces brief positional attacks and spares hearing.
High-frequency hearing loss with tinnitus and no vertigo
High-frequency loss without vertigo fits presbycusis. Meniere disease pairs hours-long episodic vertigo with LOW-frequency tinnitus, low-tone loss and aural fullness.
Episodic vertigo for hours, low-frequency tinnitus, low-tone loss, aural fullness
Correct. All four, and the LOW-frequency emphasis is what distinguishes the hearing loss from presbycusis or noise damage, which take the high frequencies first.

set2.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
set2.q: Which feature of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo separates it most cleanly from the other peripheral causes?
opts: The vertigo lasts several hours
Attacks lasting several hours describe Meniere disease. Positional vertigo attacks are measured in seconds, usually under a minute.
It follows a viral upper respiratory infection
A preceding viral upper respiratory infection points at labyrinthitis, which also takes the hearing with it — unlike positional vertigo.
There is NO hearing loss

Correct. Meniere disease and labyrinthitis both take hearing with them; this does not, because the otoconia are a vestibular problem that never touches the cochlea. Attacks also last under a minute and follow head position.
It produces aural fullness
Aural fullness is the fourth element of the Meniere tetrad. Positional vertigo produces no fullness and no hearing change at all.

set2.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set2.q: Which mechanism explains the ototoxicity of gentamicin and tobramycin?
opts: They cross-link DNA in the stria vascularis, disturbing endolymph ion homeostasis
DNA cross-linking in the stria vascularis is the mechanism of the platinum agents, cisplatin and carboplatin, which cause bilateral permanent sensorineural loss.
Reactive oxygen species destroy outer hair cells from the base, so high pitches go first
Correct. Aminoglycosides induce reactive oxygen species that selectively destroy outer hair cells, starting at the cochlear base, so high-pitch hearing is lost first.
They alter the stria vascularis potential reversibly
That is the loop diuretic effect, and reversibility is what separates it from the aminoglycosides.
They inhibit the prestin motor protein in outer hair cells
Inhibiting prestin in outer hair cells is the salicylate mechanism, and its hallmark is tinnitus rather than permanent threshold loss.

set2.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set2.q: Which description fits vocal cord nodules?
opts: Unilateral pedunculated fluid-filled growths on the middle third, from a single severe strain
That describes vocal cord POLYPS, and the unilateral-versus-bilateral split is the main distinction.
Bilateral wart-like exophytic lesions from viral infection
Viral wart-like lesions are not nodules. Nodules are bilateral fibrous calluses from chronic phonotrauma, at the junction of the anterior third.
Unilateral firm masses with cord fixation, from malignancy
Nodules are neither malignant nor fixed. They are benign bilateral symmetrical calluses from chronic phonotrauma, the cords slamming together.
Bilateral symmetrical calluses at the anterior third junction, from chronic phonotrauma
Correct. Chronic phonotrauma, the cords slamming together, causes basement membrane hyalinization, a callus. Nodules are bilateral and symmetrical at the anterior third junction.

set2.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
set2.q: Cerumen impaction, foreign bodies and canal exostoses all cause conductive loss by which of the four core mechanisms?
opts: Obstruction
Correct. A physical blockage stops sound penetrating down the canal. It is the first of four mechanisms, and the only one that acts before the sound reaches the drum.
Mass loading
That is fluid or tissue weight damping movement of the drum or ossicles — middle ear effusion, cholesteatoma.
Stiffness effect
That is impaired mobility of the ossicles or drum, of which otosclerosis is the example.
Discontinuity
That is physical disruption of the ossicular chain, from temporal bone fracture or ossicular necrosis.

set2.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
set2.q: Which time course fits the vertigo of labyrinthitis?
opts: Sudden, lasting days, improving over weeks
Correct. Labyrinthitis vertigo is sudden and lasts days, improving over weeks, unlike the hours-long attacks of Meniere disease or the sub-minute attacks of positional vertigo.
Episodic, with attacks lasting several hours
Episodic attacks lasting hours are the vertigo of Meniere disease. Labyrinthitis vertigo is sudden, lasts days and improves over weeks.
Episodic, with attacks lasting under a minute
Attacks under a minute, provoked by head position, are benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which spares hearing.
Continuous, permanent and non-improving
It is not permanent. Labyrinthitis vertigo is sudden, lasts days, and improves over the following weeks.

set2.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set2.q: In the organ of Corti, what physically opens the tip-link channels on the hair cells?
opts: Direct pressure of endolymph on the hair cell body
Endolymph displacement moves the membrane, but the channel opens because the cilia are bent against a rigid structure, not from fluid pressure on the cell.
Glutamate binding to the hair cell
Glutamate is released BY the hair cell onto cranial nerve VIII fibers after depolarization. It is the output, not the trigger.
Shearing of the stereocilia against the tectorial membrane

Correct. Basilar membrane displacement bends the stereocilia against the rigid tectorial membrane, and that mechanical deflection is what opens the channels. Everything upstream exists to produce that shear.
Stapes vibration transmitted directly to the hair cells
The stapes vibrates the oval window and starts pressure waves in the scala vestibuli. Those displace endolymph and the basilar membrane, and only the resulting shear opens the channels.

set2.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
set2.q: Which features mark vertigo as PERIPHERAL rather than central?
opts: Gradual onset, vertical nystagmus, non-suppressible, with neurological deficits
Gradual onset, vertical non-suppressible nystagmus and neurological deficits describe CENTRAL vertigo from the brainstem or cerebellum.
Gradual onset with hearing loss and tinnitus
Gradual onset is a central feature. Peripheral vertigo is sudden, with horizontal or rotational nystagmus that is fatigable and suppressed by visual fixation.
Sudden onset, horizontal or rotational nystagmus, fatigable, suppressed by visual fixation
Correct. Peripheral vertigo involves the inner ear or cranial nerve VIII, with sudden onset and prominent horizontal or rotational nystagmus that is fatigable and suppressed by visual fixation.
Absence of nystagmus entirely
Nystagmus is expected, not absent. Peripheral vertigo shows prominent horizontal or rotational nystagmus that is fatigable and suppressed by visual fixation.

set2.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
set2.q: Why does a deviated septum cause epistaxis and loss of smell?
opts: Compression of the ethmoid arteries and the olfactory nerve
Compression is not the mechanism. Turbulent air dries the mucosa into crusting and fragile vessel breakdown, and air fails to reach the cribriform plate.
Turbulent airflow dries the mucosa; air misses the cribriform plate
Correct. Two separate consequences of the same disturbed airflow: local drying with fragile vessel breakdown on one hand, and failure to deliver odorant to the superior nasal vault on the other.
Chronic infection eroding the septal vessels and olfactory epithelium
Secondary bacterial rhinosinusitis can follow ostial blockage, but the epistaxis and anosmia are explained by airflow.
Autoimmune destruction of the septal cartilage
Autoimmune destruction of septal cartilage is a different disease process; the consequences here all follow from disturbed airflow.

set2.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
set2.q: Why does a lesion of cranial nerve VIII produce the same audiometric pattern as cochlear damage?
opts: Both stiffen the ossicles
Stiffened ossicles cause conductive loss, as in otosclerosis. The cochlea and cranial nerve VIII both lie beyond the conducting chain, so both give sensorineural loss.
Both obstruct the canal
Obstruction blocks the external canal, which is a conductive mechanism rather than a sensorineural one.
Both sit beyond the conducting chain, so both give sensorineural loss
Correct. The category is defined by where the defect sits, not by which of the two structures failed.
Both add mass to the tympanic membrane
Mass loading damps the middle ear structures, which produces conductive rather than sensorineural loss.
